extracted.intended_audience: inventors, small companies, and applicants preparing patent applications (primarily US-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist-style list of common mistakes inventors make when preparing and filing patent applications, with practical warnings and corrective actions aimed at improving patentability and enforceability. Focus is on filing timing, disclosure quality, claim drafting, procedural duties, and portfolio strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Too Early
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional filed before you have actually figured out the invention buys you priority for a half-baked idea. You then spend the next year evolving the invention - and your non-provisional claims will not be supported by the provisional. Wait until you can describe the invention in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not file a provisional until you can describe the invention in sufficient detail to support later non‑provisional claims; avoid 'half‑baked' disclosures that will not provide adequate written description/enablement for later claim scope. If you plan to rely on a provisional, ensure it discloses the embodiments and variations you may later claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Too Late
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use, sale, offer for sale, or printed publication more than one year before filing is a 102(b) bar in the US (the AIA grace period was preserved for the inventor's own disclosures). In most foreign countries, any public disclosure before filing is fatal. Demos at trade shows count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File before any public disclosure to preserve foreign rights; in the US be aware of the one‑year statutory grace period but do not rely on it for foreign filings. Treat demos, trade show presentations, sales, offers for sale, and printed publications as disclosures that can destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating the Patent As a Marketing Document
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors love to write that their invention is 'revolutionary,' 'the first of its kind,' 'superior to all existing solutions.' None of these statements help patentability. They can be used by accused infringers to attack obviousness ('if you say it is revolutionary, then secondary considerations...') and 112 ('if you say it is the first, prove the prior art does not anticipate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid marketing language in the specification; focus on objective technical description and supportive evidence rather than hyperbole. Marketing statements can create problematic admissions or invite attacks on obviousness and written description/completeness under §112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient Disclosure of How It Works
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law requires enablement: a POSITA must be able to make and use the invention without undue experimentation. Inventors often describe what their invention does without describing how. A black‑box description fails enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include operational details, examples, and working parameters so a person of ordinary skill can practice the invention. Describe mechanisms, steps, materials, alternatives, and examples to avoid 'black‑box' descriptions that risk non‑enablement findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosing Only the Commercial Embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: If you only describe the version you sell, your competitors can design around with minor variations. Disclose alternatives - different materials, different geometries, different orderings, different control schemes. The spec is your safety net.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification to include multiple embodiments, variations, and alternative implementations (materials, geometries, orderings, control schemes, etc.) to broaden claim support and reduce design‑around risks. Treat the spec as a safety net for claiming variations beyond the commercialized product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letting the Inventor Write the Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Even technical inventors who can write a perfectly clear textbook chapter typically cannot write good claims. Claims have arcane drafting conventions (single‑sentence, antecedent basis, specific transitional phrases) and strategic considerations (claim differentiation, claim hierarchy, infringement‑detectability). Hire a patent attorney or registered agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have claims drafted or reviewed by an experienced patent attorney or registered agent who understands claim drafting conventions and prosecution strategy. Inventors can provide technical content, but claim language and strategy are specialized and strategic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to Update Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship is who actually conceived the claimed subject matter, not who paid for the work or who manages the team. Wrongly listing inventors can invalidate the patent. Reassess inventorship after each claim amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine inventorship based on conception of the claimed subject matter and update the inventor list whenever claims change during drafting or prosecution. Consult counsel to correct inventorship promptly when necessary to avoid invalidity risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring the Duty of Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors and attorneys have a duty (Rule 56) to disclose information material to patentability. If you know about a prior reference, disclose it via an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS). Inequitable conduct findings can render an entire patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with the duty to disclose material prior art and other information by timely submitting IDSs. Do not withhold known references; consult counsel about materiality to avoid charges of inequitable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skipping the Search
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing without a prior art search is filing blind. A $1,500 search before filing routinely surfaces references that, had they been known, would have led to a different (and stronger) claim strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a prior art search (or budget for one) before filing to inform claim scope and strategy. Use search results to shape disclosures and claims, reducing the risk of avoidable rejections or weak claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Planning the Continuation Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the first filing as the start of a portfolio, not a one‑and‑done. Plan continuations, divisionals, and foreign filings as part of an integrated budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a portfolio plan that contemplates continuations, divisionals, and international protection and aligns with commercial goals and budget. Treat the initial filing as one step in a larger prosecution and business strategy rather than a single, final filing.
